name: First-Person Perspective Analysis
description: Analyzes the frequency and contextual integration of first-person pronouns (I, me, my, we, our). AI models inherently default to an objective, third-person perspective and struggle to use first-person language organically unless explicitly forced.
mechanism: First-person pronouns are the linguistic anchor of human experience. When humans write opinions, reviews, or personal anecdotes, they naturally center themselves ('I noticed that...', 'In my experience...'). Large Language Models, conversely, are mathematically aligned (via RLHF) to act as helpful, omniscient, and objective assistants. They do not have personal experiences, bodies, or opinions, and therefore their baseline output heavily suppresses first-person language to avoid 'hallucinating a persona'. When an AI is explicitly prompted to write in the first person, it often over-corrects, either using 'I' symmetrically at the exact beginning of every sentence, or confining the first-person perspective exclusively to generic introductory clauses ('I believe that [hyper-objective fact]'). This algorithm calculates the 'Subjective Density' of the text. It measures not only the frequency of first-person pronouns but their syntactic depth. A complete lack of first-person pronouns in an inherently subjective genre (like a product review or blog post), or a highly unnatural, robotic placement of 'I' without any subjective emotional framing, strongly flags the text as machine-generated.
useCase: Crucial for verifying the authenticity of personal essays, cover letters, product reviews, and opinion pieces where the author's 'lived experience' is the core value.
strengths:
• Highly effective at detecting AI-generated reviews or personal blogs, as the model's instinct to remain objective constantly fights against the user's prompt to 'write a personal story'.
• Identains 'Persona Hallucination Fatigue'—where an AI model starts an essay using 'I', but slowly drifts back into its comfortable, objective third-person voice halfway through the text.
• Fast, lightweight, and completely immune to simple synonym-swapping techniques.
limitations:
• Entirely ineffective on academic papers, technical documentation, or journalism, where human style guides also strictly forbid the use of first-person pronouns.
• Humans who write in a highly formal, detached 'corporate' tone may trigger false positives.
• Very easy for humans to manually 'patch' AI text by simply inserting 'I think' or 'In my opinion' throughout the document.
parameters:
Analysis: Pronoun Frequency Extraction & Syntactic Placement
Metric: Ratio of Subjective First-Person Framing vs Objective Declarations
Output: 0-100 Pronoun Sterility (Subjective Detachment) Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 75-85% in casual, narrative, and persuasive texts. It acts as a powerful behavioral polygraph for 'objective detachment' mandated by AI safety alignment.

references.title: Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
Guo, B. et al. (2023). How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection. NeurIPS.
